questions.text: Because the platform holds strong compliance credentials and a high privacy rating, teachers may enter real student names and details when generating materials.
questions.explanation: The protections are real, but the lesson keeps the standard practice unchanged: use placeholders such as "Student A" or fictional names rather than real names, specific diagnoses or sensitive family information.

questions.text: What does Raina, the built-in chat assistant, change about revising a generated draft?

options.text: You can ask for a specific change to one part of the output instead of regenerating the whole thing.
It applies your school's branding and style guide to every output automatically.
It replaces the guided forms, so every task then starts from a blank chat box.
It stores your previous answers so a form never has to be filled in twice.

questions.explanation: Raina turns a one-shot generator into an iterative conversation — in the worked example it added a simpler cut-and-paste version of one activity while leaving the rest of the lesson plan intact.

questions.text: Which of these does the lesson show the platform actually doing?

options.text: Producing a lesson plan that respects stated constraints such as limited lab equipment and a 45-minute period
Generating comprehension questions from the transcript of a video, complete with answer keys
Producing content in languages other than English when the language is specified
Recording and transcribing your classroom lessons automatically
Verifying that the facts in its output are correct before you see them

questions.explanation: The worked examples show a constrained, differentiated lesson plan and a video-based quiz with answer keys, and the lesson notes that content can be generated in Croatian, Greek or Romanian; fact-checking is explicitly left to the teacher.

questions.text: The lesson compares a general assistant to a well-stocked kitchen and this platform to a recipe app. What point is the comparison making?

options.text: The platform asks you the specific questions it needs answered and structures the request for you, whereas a general assistant leaves the whole prompt to you.
The platform writes better prose than a general assistant on any task you give it.
The platform is meant to replace general assistants entirely in a teacher's workflow.
The platform needs no information about your class, because its tools already know what teachers require.

questions.explanation: A guided form supplies the structure of the request so you contribute the classroom detail instead of composing a prompt from scratch; the lesson is explicit that both approaches have their place, and that the more you put into the Additional Context field the better the output.
